cards.front: What are the four zones around your car, and how far ahead should you scan?
cards.back: Map the zones: green ahead, blue beside, yellow blind spots, red behind; keep eyes moving with scans ten seconds ahead to buy reaction time and dodge last-second moves.

cards.front: What following gap should you hold, and how do you handle a tailgater?
cards.back: Tailgating blinds and compresses reactions, so hold three seconds, lift off when cut off, and widen gaps for tailgaters behind by holding course then merging right, plus room behind bikes on metal and gravel.

cards.front: How do the zones, the ten-second scan and the three-second rule work together?
cards.back: Zone colors split attention four ways with ten-second scans buying time, while the three-second rule converts tailgating pressure into gap management through lifting off, holding course, and merging right.

cards.front: How should you manage the space at your sides?
cards.back: Mind the flanks: shun others' blind spots, never pace alongside, open room for freeway mergers even holding priority, space off parked cars, and look both ways even facing red lights and stop signs.

cards.front: Where are blind spots, and how do you check them?
cards.back: Blind spots sit beside and slightly behind the driver; check with shoulder glances that move only the head before lane changes, turns, merges, backing, departures, parking moves, curb pullouts, and door openings.

cards.front: How do side discipline and your own blind-spot checks fit together?
cards.back: Flank discipline means avoiding others' blind spots and refusing to pace, while own-blind-spot checks fire by shoulder glance before eight distinct maneuvers from lane changes to door openings.

cards.front: When should you check behind you?
cards.back: Rear checks defeat rear-enders: sweep mirrors and turn the head when changing lanes, checking blinds, slowing, turning into drives, parking, working curbs, and backing.

cards.front: When should you use and dim high beams, and which lights go on in rain?
cards.back: Run high beams on dark open roads while stopping inside the lit stretch, dim for oncoming traffic, and when blinded look right or aside without retaliating; rain means low beams never parking lights alone.

cards.front: What extra care does night driving need?
cards.back: Night walkers, riders, and work zones demand extra care and slower speeds, eyes need adjustment time leaving bright places, and single approaching lights demand a far-right berth for bikes, motos, or dead lamps.

cards.front: How do rear checks, high beams, rain and night hazards fit together?
cards.back: Rear checks mirror side checks across seven triggers, high beams trade distance against blinding with look-aside recovery, rain forces low beams, and night singles out walkers, work zones, adjustment lag, and one-light mysteries.

cards.front: How do you fight glare?
cards.back: Fight glare with clean glass, polarized shades, roomy gaps, a working visor, pedestrian watchfulness, and avoiding sunrise and sunset runs.

cards.front: What causes skids, and how do you prevent and handle them?
cards.back: Skids mean lost traction; ice and snow skid hardest when fast or downhill, so slow early for curves, shun fast turns and stops, drop gears before descents, dodge slick patches, and in a skid lift off, skip brakes, steer into it, seek dry pavement.

cards.front: How do the glare fixes and skid responses compare?
cards.back: Glare fights back with glass, shades, gaps, visors, and timing, while skids split into slippery-surface slides answered by lifting, brake-skipping, steering-in, and dry-pavement hunting.

cards.front: How do you brake out of a locked-wheel skid with each brake type?
cards.back: Locked skids follow hard fast braking; four-wheel ABS takes firm pressure, rear ABS eases to rolling then steers into the skid, front ABS releases and straightens, ABS-less cars pump, sunk pedals pump gently with downshifts and emergency brakes, wet brakes dry under gas plus brake.

cards.front: How much should you slow on wet, snowy and icy roads?
cards.back: Wet roads cut five to ten miles per hour, packed snow halves speed, ice caps at five; shade hides ice that freezes first and dries last, bridges freeze first, and first rain on dry oily pavement demands instant slowing.

cards.front: How do ABS types and road surfaces change your braking and speed?
cards.back: Locked skids answer ABS type with firm, eased, or released pedals against pump-and-downshift fallbacks, while slippery roads staircase down by surface: wet shaves miles, snow halves, ice crawls at five, with shade and bridges freezing first.

cards.front: What limits and steps apply when driving in a storm?
cards.back: Storms cap sight near one hundred feet and speed at thirty; run wipers, low beams, and defroster, clear mud and snow off glass and lights, and carry correct chains in snow country.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and what should you do when it happens?
cards.back: Hydroplaning floats the car on water with zero road contact, so slight inputs trigger spins; prevent with slow speeds, water dodging, slosh heeding, and gentle lane moves, and when floating ease off without touching brakes.

cards.front: How do you get out of snow or mud?
cards.back: Escape snow and mud with low gears and straight wheels, gentle unsprung gas, forward-reverse rocking to freedom, and boards or branches under the tires only while stopped.

cards.front: How do storms, hydroplaning and getting unstuck compare?
cards.back: Storm blindness pairs the hundred-foot sight line with the thirty cap plus wipers, lights, defroster, and chains, hydroplaning floats into brake-free easing, and snow burial answers rocking and traction aids.

cards.front: What dangers do flooded roads hide, and how should you respond?
cards.back: Floods threaten sweep-off, debris, collapse, breakdowns, and electrocution with unreadable depths; deep water means rerouting, forced crossings go slow, and brakes get tested right after.

cards.front: How should you drive in high winds?
cards.back: High winds menace tall rigs most; slow down, grip firmly, watch for debris, shun cruise control, and pull over to wait out the worst.

cards.front: How do flood and wind responses compare?
cards.back: Floods stack five distinct killers behind unreadable depths with rerouting beating slow crossings and post-water brake tests mandatory, while winds slow tall rigs into firm grips without cruise.

cards.front: What should you do in fog or smoke?
cards.back: Fog and smoke favor postponement; forced trips go slow on low beams never parking lights, stop inside sight distance, widen gaps, wipe and defog, hold lanes, listen for hidden traffic, and pull off with flashers when too thick.

cards.front: How do you follow a patrol traffic break?
cards.back: Traffic breaks weave patrol lights to clear hazards, fog jams, and crash risks; drivers flash along, match the officer's gentle pace at distance, and never pass until lights die and conditions clear.

cards.front: How do fog driving and traffic breaks compare?
cards.back: Fog forces low-beam patience inside sight distance with pull-off flashers as the escape, while traffic breaks convert patrol weaves into follower flashers, matched pacing, and no-passing discipline.

cards.front: Who must wear seat belts, and why do belts matter in a crash?
cards.back: Belts bind everyone with tickets for skippers and drivers answering for unbelted under-sixteens; crash physics keeps bodies flying at travel speed into glass and across seats, belts holding position and softening blows.

cards.front: How should a seat belt be worn, including during pregnancy?
cards.back: Belt right: shoulder strap snug across chest never under arms or behind backs, lap belt low on hips against submarining, pregnancy routing the lap low under the belly and the strap between breasts past the bulge.

cards.front: How do belt law, crash physics and correct belt fit connect?
cards.back: Belt law binds riders and drivers alike with under-sixteen liability, crash physics explains the flying body and cross-seat sling, and correct wear routes straps across chest and low hips with pregnancy detours.

cards.front: How must children ride, by age and size?
cards.back: Kids ride approved restraints by size: under two, forty pounds, three-four height ride rear-facing never before airbags; under eight or four-nine ride restrained in back with narrow front exceptions; eight or four-nine graduates to standard belts, installs checked by pros.

cards.front: What are the stages of child restraints?
cards.back: Child restraints staircase by size: rear-facing infants with no front airbag exposure, back-seat boosters with six narrow front exceptions, then standard belts at eight or four-nine, with pro install checks.

cards.front: How far should you sit from the airbag cover?
cards.back: Airbags assist belts; drivers and passengers sit ten inches off the covers measured chest to wheel, dealers advising the cramped, and children beside side bags face grave risk.

cards.front: What are the rules on leaving children or animals in cars?
cards.back: Never leave six-and-under alone in cars with supervisors twelve-plus required, and never cook kids or animals in hot parked cars whose heat spikes even on cracked windows toward dehydration, heatstroke, and death.

cards.front: What does the Basic Speed Law say, and what are the default limits?
cards.back: The Basic Speed Law bans speeds unsafe for conditions regardless of signs, weighing traffic, surfaces, walkers, weather, and congestion without freeway weaving; defaults cap at sixty-five on highways, fifty-five on two-lane roads and while towing.

cards.front: What links airbag distance, child supervision and the speed law?
cards.back: Airbags demand ten-inch standoffs for all seats with dealer help for the cramped, children stay out of hot cars and solo sits under twelve-plus supervision, and the Basic Speed Law caps judgment at sixty-five and fifty-five defaults.

cards.front: When two hazards appear together, how do you handle them?
cards.back: Split dangers by severity: bike versus oncoming means slowing, yielding the lane to the car, then passing the bike with three feet or using the left lane against steady flows.

cards.front: What should you do when a tire blows out?
cards.back: Blowouts forbid panic braking or lifting; grip with both hands, hold speed while safe, ease off the gas, steer straight to stabilize, look where you want to go, then slow and pull off.

cards.front: What should you do if your wheels leave the pavement?
cards.back: Pavement departures need a firm grip, foot off gas, gentle braking, a rear check, and a careful reentry, never violent yanks toward oncoming traffic.

cards.front: How do dual hazards, blowouts and pavement departures compare?
cards.back: Dual hazards resolve by severity with bikes getting three feet after oncoming clears, blowouts forbid panic inputs in favor of grip, hold, ease, and steer-straight, and pavement departures reenter gently without violent yanks.

cards.front: What should you watch for in heat waves and cold snaps?
cards.back: Heat waves demand gauge watching, no sustained speeding, and air conditioning off; cold snaps demand gauge watching for antifreeze gaps plus defrosting or cracked windows, manuals holding details.

cards.front: What should you do if your car fails on the freeway?
cards.back: Freeway failures pull fully right, exit and reenter from the right, call five-eleven or find a box, return quickly, stay belted inside with flashers as needed, abandoning the car only for missing shoulders, guardrails, or true refuges.

cards.front: What free help do freeway patrols give, and what do they not do?
cards.back: Commute-hour freeway patrols give free gas gallons, jumps, radiator patches, flat changes, crash reports, and free tows to approved spots when dead, refusing private tows, shop tips, motorcycles, and crashes unless directed, all via five-eleven.

cards.front: How do temperature extremes, freeway failures and patrol help fit together?
cards.back: Temperature extremes split gauge watching between speed-plus-AC discipline and antifreeze-plus-defrost care, freeway failures pull right with right-side exits, five-eleven calls, belted waiting, and rare abandonment, and patrols cover gas, jumps, patches, flats, reports, and tows minus privates, tips, bikes, and crashes.

cards.front: Your car is stuck on tracks with a train coming and lights flashing. What do you do?
cards.back: Trapped on tracks facing a train with flashers: exit instantly, run diagonally away toward the train's origin side, then call emergency services.

cards.front: Your car is stuck on tracks with no train or flashers. What do you do?
cards.back: Trapped with no train or flashers: exit, call the posted crossing number with the crossing ID to report the car, then call emergency services.

cards.front: What are the rules on phones and distractions while driving?
cards.back: Distraction kills through phones, navigation, kids, pets, music, and grooming; handheld use is illegal, adults go hands-free only when needed, calls wait for voicemail or pullouts, texts and emails wait always.

cards.front: How do track escapes split, and what does distraction law ban?
cards.back: Track entrapment splits on train presence: flashers mean instant exit with diagonal runs toward the train side plus emergency calls, silence means posted-number calls with crossing IDs first; distraction law bans handhelds with hands-free-only adults and zero-tolerance texts.

cards.front: Where may a phone be mounted, and what rule applies to minors?
cards.back: Mount phones on glass, dash, or console clear of sight lines for single-swipe use only; minors face a total wireless ban behind the wheel except emergency calls.

cards.front: How do driver assistance systems and self-driving vehicles react?
cards.back: Assistance systems and self-drivers react non-humanly, so expect alien responses to road events.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous, and which symptoms call for an exhaust check?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide kills odorlessly from exhaust pipes, so never idle in closed garages; tiredness, yawning, dizziness, nausea, headaches, and ringing ears all demand an exhaust check.

cards.front: What links phone mounting, assistance systems and carbon monoxide?
cards.back: Phone rules pair mounted single-swipe use for adults against total minor bans except emergencies, assistance systems warn of alien reactions, and carbon monoxide pairs closed-garage bans with a six-symptom watchlist ending in exhaust checks.

recap_hooks.text: Scan ten seconds ahead, keep three seconds behind the car ahead, keep room at your sides, and glance over your shoulder for blind spots.
Check behind with mirrors and a head turn, dim high beams for oncoming traffic, use low beams in rain, and take extra care at night.
Fight glare with clean glass and shades, steer into a skid without braking, and brake by ABS type in a locked skid.
Wet roads cut five to ten miles per hour, packed snow halves speed, and ice caps at five.
Storms cap speed at thirty, hydroplaning means easing off without braking, and deep floods mean rerouting.
Slow down in wind, fog and smoke, use low beams, and never pass during a patrol traffic break.
Everyone buckles, drivers answer for unbelted passengers under sixteen, and children ride in approved restraints by size.
Sit ten inches from the airbag, never leave children six and under alone, and drive at a speed safe for conditions.
In a blowout grip the wheel and steer straight, and after leaving the pavement reenter gently.
On a freeway breakdown pull fully right and call five-eleven, where patrols give free help.
Stuck on tracks with a train coming, get out and run diagonally toward the train's side; with no train, call the posted number.
Handheld phone use is illegal, minors may not use wireless devices at all except emergencies, and carbon monoxide symptoms call for an exhaust check.
